items.title: A Roman Cup and Hundreds of Other Treasures Unearthed in This 2,000-Year-Old Tomb Reveal the Rich Exchange Network of an Ancient Asian Empire
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The Xiongnu people dominated Central Asia for some 300 years. Now, a grave discovered in Mongolia has revealed the pastoral culture’s links to the Roman Empire, Han China and the Lelang Commandery

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Meilan Solly
A gourd-shaped pendant discovered in the tomb

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Some 2,000 years ago, an elite individual associated with the nomadic Xiongnu Empire was buried in style in what is now northeastern Mongolia. Their tomb, measuring nearly 240 feet in length (about four-fifths the height of the Statue of Liberty), is the largest of its kind discovered in the East Asian country to date.

Despite this impressive exterior, the tomb’s interior is surprisingly small and shallow. But it was packed with treasures that shed new light on the Xiongnu people’s links to such far-flung foreign powers as the Roman Empire and the Lelang Commandery , an administrative division of China’s Han dynasty that was based in what is now Korea.

The National Museum of Korea , the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia recently completed a four-year excavation of the burial, which is known officially as Tomb 160 . It’s located in Duurlig Nars , a Xiongnu burial ground with some 300 graves.

Archaeologists recovered 413 artifacts from the tomb, including a glass cup believed to be of Roman origin, a gourd-shaped silver pendant that once adorned a horse’s harness, a lacquered chariot and 15 jade pieces modeled after Han funerary goods .

The pendant resembles accessories found in Lelang tombs in modern-day North Korea, but unlike those ornaments, it boasts a crystal at its center. The jade objects, meanwhile, were fashioned in irregular shapes with intricate designs carved onto their surfaces, setting them apart from the disc-shaped bi prized by the Han as symbols of heaven.

“This excavation clearly shows that the Xiongnu of 2,000 years ago were linked to a broad exchange network reaching from Rome to the Korean Peninsula,” the National Museum of Korea says in a statement , per a translation by Seoul Economic Daily . “We expect it to serve as a turning point in expanding the field of Korean archaeology into Eurasia.”

The rich range of objects buried alongside the deceased testifies to their high status. Although the researchers have yet to identify the grave’s occupant, they plan to conduct a DNA analysis of teeth and hair recovered from the individual’s coffin to determine their sex and age.

To construct the tomb, ancient laborers built an elevated terrace enclosed by nine layers of stacked stones. The central chamber of the grave extends to a depth of nearly 50 feet, making it significantly smaller than comparable Xiongnu tombs in central Mongolia, whose depths reach more than 70 feet. The excavation team suggests that this downsized interior reflects societal shifts in the late first and second centuries C.E., when the tomb was built. At the time, the Xiongnu Empire was declining , with internal disagreements and external pressure from the Han military weakening the once-great pastoral confederation.

The Xiongnu thrived in Central Asia between the third century B.C.E. and the second century C.E., wielding control over vast swaths of territory “without building cities, forming central bureaucracies, devising a writing system or mobilizing masses of farmers to produce food,” Bruce Bower wrote for Science News in 2023. In recent years, scholars have revealed an array of insights on the Xiongnu that challenge long-held perceptions of the group as “ barbaric ” invaders.

In 2023, for example, a paper published in the journal Science Advances suggested that elite Xiongnu women traveled to the empire’s frontiers to shore up alliances with powerful locals. “They are representatives of the imperial clan that ruled the empire,” study co-author Bryan Miller , an archaeologist at the University of Michigan, told Live Science ’s Tom Metcalfe. “You’ve got these marriage alliances spanning the whole empire, even in these local communities.”

Speaking with Science News , Miller added, “This must have been an empire organized around moving populations. Xiongnu elites were savvy politicians who delegated power to keep the empire together.”

Meilan Solly is a senior associate digital editor at Smithsonian magazine, where she oversees the online history section and writes about everything from archaeology to the British royal family. Solly’s specialties are Tudor England, Renaissance and modern art, and World War II.

items.title: Rembrandt's 'Night Watch' Is Teeming With Life. Researchers Reveal a Hidden World of Microbes All Over the Masterpiece
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Samples swabbed from the 17th-century painting reveal myriad microorganisms, including one perplexing bacterium that was first discovered at a Japanese sugar refinery in 2013

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
TNW
sampling the painting

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For nearly four centuries, viewers have admired the bustling militia figures frozen in oil paint on Rembrandt van Rijn ’s 1642 masterpiece, The Night Watch . Now, scientists in Amsterdam have revealed that the iconic canvas is teeming with an invisible, living world of its own.

Researchers from the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia (which claims to be the world’s only museum dedicated to microbes) are collecting 60 samples from 10 different areas of the painting to catalog its surface microbiome. Early laboratory cultures have turned up myriads of common bacteria and one puzzling outlier: Microbacterium saccharophilum , a bacterial species first identified in 2013 at a sugar refinery in Japan.

“This is the first time The Night Watch , or any work of art, has been analyzed in this way, and we’ve found bacteria that appear on human skin and in soil, and are even associated with plants,” Eline van Bloois , a microbiologist at Artis-Micropia tells El País ’ Isabel Ferrer.

The ongoing investigation is featured in “ The Night Watch Lives ,” an exhibition at ARTIS-Micropia running through May 2027. Centered around a life-size reproduction of Rembrandt’s painting marked with numbered sampling dates, the display showcases living bacterial colonies growing inside glass-encased Petri dishes.

“To get that close to the painting was very scary,” van Bloois tells Hyperallergic 's Noëlle de Leeuw. “After all, it's a piece of art that is so well-known to so many people.”

The microbial census forms a new chapter of “ Operation Night Watch ,” the Rijksmuseum’s sweeping research and conservation initiative launched in 2019. Inside a glass chamber in the museum’s Gallery of Honor , conservators are currently working in full view of visitors to painstakingly remove a yellowed layer of varnish applied in the 1970s. It’s a delicate process, using organic-fabric gauze, small tissues and tiny amounts of solvent that will take years to complete.

Decades before Dutch microbiologist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first described microorganisms in the 1670s, Rembrandt was already using chemistry to protect his work against microscopic threats. Previous Operation Night Watch analyses revealed that Rembrandt had applied a layer of lead-laden oil beneath the primer to shield the painting from moisture and mold in Amsterdam’s damp buildings. The canvas was later trimmed in 1715 to fit inside Amsterdam City Hall and has suffered numerous conservation treatments and deep cleanings roughly once every 50 years.

Since 2019, Operation Night Watch has made several other breakthroughs. Researchers restored the trimmed edges of the painting with artificial intelligence and discovered a hidden sketch beneath the paint with advanced X-ray imaging.

“Thirty or 40 years ago, nobody could have imagined you’d be talking to a chemist or biologist about The Night Watch ,” Rijksmuseum director Taco Dibbits said during a press conference, Hyperallergic reports . “And I think precisely because this research is broadening—the fact that the humanities and the exact sciences are collaborating—it also leads to it becoming more widely embraced.”

To sample the 400-year-old surface safely, conservators and lab technicians gently pressed small, sterile cellulose discs against both varnished and unvarnished sections of the canvas. Those discs were transferred to Petri dishes and incubated in ARTIS-Micropia’s laboratory until invisible microbes multiplied into visible colonies, which an external lab then identified.

The team has completed only half of its six planned sampling trips to the Rijksmuseum so far, with 20 identified microbes currently on display and another 10 still incubating. Researchers expect to collect all 60 samples by February.

Among the familiar microbial residents detected so far are Staphylococcus epidermidis and Micrococcus luteus , harmless bacteria routinely found on human skin that help hydrate it and defend against pathogens, Amsterdamian ’s Dana Marin reports. The team also isolated plant-root and soil species, including Kocuria palustris , Kocuria rhizophila and Lysinibacillus sphaericus , a resilient bacterium capable of surviving harsh environments rich in heavy metals.

None of those, however, baffled scientists quite like Microbacterium saccharophilum , which turned up on a section where old varnish had already been stripped away. Originally isolated from soil at the Ensuiko Sugar Refining plant in Yokohama, Japan, the microbe has no obvious connection to a Dutch Golden Age canvas.

“We’ve seen very little sugar in Rembrandt’s painting so far, and it’s best not to speculate, but it’s possible that the Saccharophilum isn’t as old as the canvas,” van Bloois tells El País , adding that scientists currently have no way to determine when any of the bacteria arrived.

items.title: For the First Time, Astronomers Witnessed a Giant Star Gobble Up Its Smaller Stellar Companion
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The merger caused an eruption in late 2025, which researchers rushed to document using several ground- and space-based telescopes. With older data and the help of computer simulations, the team reconstructed the entire astrophysical process

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Margherita Bassi
the merger within the broader Andromeda galaxy

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In 2023, astronomers realized that a red giant star in our neighboring Andromeda galaxy was doing something strange. Sure enough, two years later, the astronomical object exploded.

The researchers rushed to observe the phenomenon, and they sifted through older data to piece together what had happened. Analyses suggest the huge star had gobbled up its smaller stellar companion, marking the first direct observation of this kind of star merger. The findings were described November 18 in the journal Nature .

The eruption, called AT 2025abao, occurred because the two stars shared what’s called a common envelope. Some stars approaching the end of their lives balloon to a huge size, entering a giant phase. As an object expands , its outer layer of gas—or envelope—engulfs anything orbiting it, resulting in odd interactions.

However, common envelopes are tough to observe because they happen over relatively short timescales of months to years, and usually, just a few stars exist in this phase at a time within a galaxy, writes Jason Nordhaus , an astrophysicist at the Rochester Institute of Technology who did not participate in the work, in commentary accompanying the study.

Experts estimate that nearly a third of all stars go through a common envelope phase at some point during their lives, reports New Scientist.

To investigate the strange event, which occurred in October 2025, researchers obtained data captured just 47 days later by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope . They also had follow-up observations from other ground- and space-based instruments, as well as data from roughly the past 30 years, which revealed the big star had started brightening in 2018.

Using all that data, the team was able to “reconstruct what happened with quite significant confidence,” Sven Buder , an astrophysicist at the Australian National University who did not participate in the study, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation ’s Jacinta Bowler.

Computer simulations hinted that the two stars had orbited each other for millennia. Before the eye-catching explosion, the primary star—dubbed “Big Bao” after the eruption’s name—had become enormous. It was seven times more massive, 350 times the radius and 18,000 times brighter than our sun. Its companion, “Little Bao,” on the other hand, probably contained 0.7 times the mass of our sun and was smaller and fainter.

The smaller star spiraled into the bigger one’s envelope, and the two objects took about seven years to unite, which is quite quick in astronomical terms. The merger occurred when the red giant dragged its companion into its core, resulting in a dramatic event resembling “a bomb exploding inside a living star,” study co-author Kishalay De , an astrophysicist at Columbia University, says in a statement .

“We were able to see all different phases of this process—we were able to see the quiescent system, we were able to see the moment the stars touched each other, we were able to see the inspiral, and we were able to see the big outburst in 2025,” lead author Viraj Karambelkar , also an astrophysicist at Columbia University, tells New Scientist ’s Leah Crane. “So we now know how this process works far better than we ever had before.”

Now, however, the system is too dusty for scientists to observe the aftermath directly, and it will likely remain so for years, reports Science News ’ Meghan Bartels. In the meantime, Karambelkar says they can work to “catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”

Margherita Bassi is a freelance journalist and trilingual storyteller. Her work has appeared in publications including BBC Travel, Discover magazine, Live Science , Atlas Obscura and Hidden Compass .

items.title: An Isolated Group of Amazonian Hunter-Gatherers Made a Rare Request for Help From Outsiders, Raising Concerns About Forest Degradation
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Around 20 members of the Indigenous Awá tribe emerged from the rainforest and received food from neighboring villagers. The group has not made contact with the outside world in decades, so experts say deforestation may have left these individuals with no other option

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For decades, the Awá , an Indigenous tribe in the Brazilian Amazon rainforest, has lived in almost complete isolation from the modern world. That changed on November 16, when a group of around 20 men, women and children emerged from the forest’s edge.

The Awá individuals, some of whom carried spears or wore necklaces and headdresses, made contact with a government agency that supports Indigenous peoples and the Guajajara , a larger, non-isolated Indigenous group that lives adjacent to the Awá. Both reside in Brazil’s Arariboia Indigenous Territory in the northeast state of Maranhão . Guajajara members captured photos and videos of the encounter, which have been shared by the London-based Indigenous advocacy group Survival International.

The interaction lasted for several hours, Stephen Gibbs reports for the London Times , though the two groups spoke different languages, rendering communication almost impossible. Near the end, the Guajajara shared yams with the Awá, who took the offering and, smiling, retreated among the trees.

However, Guajajara spokesperson Olimpio Santos Guajajara warns this should not be taken as a heartwarming story but as a worrying sign about the sustainability of the Awá’s voluntary isolation.

“We were trying to avoid contact with them,” he tells Brazil’s Globo television network, per the London Times . Since the late 1980s, the national government has followed a no-contact policy regarding isolated tribes like the Awá, allowing the Indigenous peoples to remain away from modern society at their discretion. “Unfortunately, today they felt forced to come and make contact,” Santos says.

Sarah Shenker , head of Survival International’s Brazil office, says the pressures of illicit deforestation, cattle ranching and hunting might be pushing the tribe to its limits, forcing them to emerge from isolation to survive.

“They’ve shown so clearly for so long that they don’t want contact with outsiders,” she tells the New York Times ’ Zane Irwin. “The fact that they’ve come out now does indicate they’ve probably felt forced to. … Because their lives are so intricately related to the forest, it would be impossible to completely separate the pressures on the land.”

The Brazilian government has designated certain swaths of the Amazon , including Arariboia, as protected Indigenous land. But as deforestation and farm development have increased, these small territories are one of the few places still home to the Amazon’s historic hardwoods, Shenker tells the Times .

Thanks to conservation efforts and renewed enforcement , deforestation is slowing in Brazil. Still, estimates suggest that nearly 20 percent of the Amazon, which spans several South American countries, has been destroyed since the 1970s, and the forest can’t handle much more .

At least 196 uncontacted tribes live in ten countries worldwide, according to Survival International. Roughly 95 percent reside in the Amazon rainforest.

In recent years, hunters, loggers and ranchers have increasingly encroached upon the Awá territory. They previously cut down over 34 percent of one legally protected Awá reserve. Survival International says the Brazilian government has hardly responded to these intrusions. In its place, a team of Guajajara people known as the Forest Guardians has taken to defending the Arariboia territory, and several members have died during these conflicts.

Repeated hunting and deforestation pose significant strain to the Awá way of life. The tribe survives off the forest, hunting wild boar, deer, monkeys and fish, and gathering fruit and honey, according to the Times . The forest is also central to the people’s medicinal and spiritual practices. But this is only possible in an “ever-smaller island of Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” says Caroline Pearce , director of Survival International, in a statement .

When the Awá made contact with the Guajajara village, the effects of this habitat loss were clear: Uirá Garcia , an anthropologist at the Federal University of São Paulo who has studied the isolated tribe for 20 years, tells Globo that some members of the group looked “exceptionally thin,” per the London Times . This was particularly concerning given the timing of the encounter in the middle of the Amazon’s rainy season—typically a time of abundance in the forest.

Experts also worried that contact with the modern world may pose serious health risks to the Awá. They have not received any vaccinations or built immunity to common viruses like influenza, measles and chicken pox, making them vulnerable to any pathogens present in the Guajajara population. Introduced diseases are currently the primary killer of isolated tribal people.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness. Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.

The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram.

items.title: Nine-Pound Eagles Seem to Be Hunting 60-Pound Baboons in Africa—Hinting the Predators May Have Gone After Our Ancestors, Too
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: In northeastern Chad, researchers found evidence of Verreaux's eagles attacking full-grown olive baboons weighing as much as a small human. The findings suggest early hominins had to watch out for ambushes from the sky, which may have shaped their evolution

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
An illustration of a large bird approaching a baboon, next to an image of a baboon skull with an eagle claw

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Eagles are formidable aerial predators capable of taking down animals much larger than themselves, including primates. But scientists have long believed that eagles tend to go after smaller primates, generally weighing less than 30 pounds.

New research suggests otherwise. Scientists have found evidence of Verreaux’s eagles hunting full-grown olive baboons weighing nearly 60 pounds, which they describe in a study published November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology .

The findings add to scientists’ understanding of predator-prey relationships. But they also raise the intriguing new possibility that eagle attacks might have influenced human evolution. Some of our ancestors, such as Australopithecus afarensis , weighed about as much as modern baboons, so it’s plausible that eagles went after them, too, millions of years ago. The threat of these attacks, researchers posit, might have affected how early humans communicated and cooperated with one another.

In February and March 2025, primatologists went looking for olive baboons on the Ennedi Plateau , a remote area in northeastern Chad filled with sandstone cliffs, gorges and rock formations. They were hoping to collect genetic samples so they could chart the history of the baboons’ movement across Africa.

But the focus of their expedition took an unexpected turn when they stumbled upon an olive baboon skull with a distinctive hole at the back of one of the eye sockets—clear evidence that a razor-sharp eagle talon had speared the primate’s head. The researchers had noticed Verreaux’s eagles soaring overhead, but it hadn’t occurred to them that the birds might be going after the baboons.

During that initial trip, they recovered the remains of nine olive baboons, including eight adult males. Two of the skulls had talon-shaped puncture marks, while one shoulder blade was covered in what appeared to be talon scratch marks. In June 2026, they found another skull and partial skeleton, which also showed signs of eagle predation.

The study authors can’t definitively rule out scavenging. But “the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” they write in the paper.

Further supporting the idea that Verreaux’s eagles were actively hunting the baboons, not just scavenging their remains, the scientists noted how groups of baboons responded whenever the birds got close, based on previously published observations. As soon as Verreaux’s eagles came into view, the primates started warning each other with alarm calls and taking cover. The baboons didn’t behave this way when other big birds of prey were nearby, suggesting they viewed the Verreaux’s eagles—which typically max out at about nine pounds—as legitimate threats.

“At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t,” study co-author Nathaniel Dominy , a primatologist at Dartmouth College, says in a statement . “Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”

The scientists estimate that, when they were alive, the baboons whose remains they initially discovered weighed approximately 49 pounds on average. But the one found in 2026 appears to have been much heavier, possibly weighing as much as 58 pounds. That’s well within the range of early hominin species: “ Lucy ,” the famous A. afarensis individual who lived in what is now Ethiopia roughly 3.2 million years ago, is believed to have weighed about 62 pounds.

The only known case of an eagle hunting and killing an ancient hominin is the Taung Child , reports Live Science . The A. africanus individual is estimated to have been about 3 at death, and their skull contains puncture marks at the bottom of the eye sockets.

Scientists know that our ancestors were vulnerable to attacks from ground-based predators like crocodiles and hyenas. But the new findings suggest they might also have needed to be on alert for ambushes from the sky.

That could have affected their behavior. Modern primates that live in areas with predatory eagles tend to move around in large groups made up of various primate species. “That means extra competition for the food—but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost,” lead author Catherine Hobaiter , a primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, tells Live Science ’s Owen Jarus.

Perhaps our ancestors deployed a similar strategy, learning to cooperate, rather than compete, with other hominin and primate species because they discovered there’s safety in numbers. They might also have evolved other adaptations in response to potential eagle attacks, such as calling out to warn others or living in places where they could easily hide.

items.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
items.author: Ben Brubaker
items.summary: When links in a communication network go down, messages can get routed in a loop. Computer scientists now know that four simple network structures are to blame. The post Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’ first appeared on Quanta Magazine

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.

Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.

If a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.

Now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They showed that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.

“It’s a very elegant contribution,” said Michael Schapira , a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”

Imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?

The first router for Arpanet, the predecessor of the internet.

One simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.

In principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.

This restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.

In a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each new packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.

With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” said Brighten Godfrey , a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.

In 2020, Stefan Schmid and his colleagues proved a partial result about the reliability of communication networks.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For millennia, roses have been capturing the admiration of humans, who have shown their appreciation for the flower in myriad ways. Poems, songs, nursery rhymes and more have praised the plant. Among some European nobles, roses and rose water were once so precious that they were considered legal tender. Vincent van Gogh has immortalized them on canvas.

President Ronald Reagan named it America’s national flower in 1986. “We hold the rose dear as the symbol of life and love and devotion, of beauty and eternity,” Regan wrote in his official proclamation.

Likewise, these Smithsonian Magazine Photo Contest entrants considered the flower worthy of their artistic attention. Take a look.

Donny Bajohr is the associate photography editor at Smithsonian . You can follow him on Instagram @donny_bajohr .

Tracy Scott Forson is a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine.

Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson, Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.

Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it. Explore a larger archive on Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
recently completed a Master of Divinity postgraduate degree at Harvard Divinity School, focusing on comparative religion and sacred landscapes. She is originally from Bangor, Maine.

In October 1948, in Country Kerry, Ireland, Seán Ó Muircheartaigh met with Seosamh Ó Dálaigh to tell him about the woman who came from the sea. She had appeared, said Ó Muircheartaigh, one night on the magharees, those bright spits of sand that occasionally pop up amid the rain-lashed rocks of the Dingle peninsula. Alone on the beach, she settled herself on a rock and began combing her hair.

Also on the beach was a farmer, who – much to the surprise of the woman herself – would by daybreak become her husband. He’d come to gather seaweed, seeing her before she saw him. Beautiful as she was, the woman was also strange: the creature he saw stagger onto that Dingle beach was not a woman at all. It was a seal.

By the time Ó Muircheartaigh told Ó Dálaigh about the seal woman, he was already 80. He had been born in the apocalyptic aftermath of the Great Hunger that divested as much as a third of Ireland’s population to death or migration, and he had survived two great wars. Most of the disappeared were – like Ó Muircheartaigh himself – small farmers and native Irish, or Gaeilge, speakers. The famine had been not just a physical genocide: it had been a linguistic and cultural one, too.

Both Ó Muircheartaigh and Ó Dálaigh were veteran contributors to the Irish Folklore Commission: the former as a renowned storyteller; the latter, an equally renowned collector. The IFC is now the National Folklore Collection at University College Dublin ­– a behemoth of 3 million pages of texts and recordings. But in 1948, following eight centuries of colonialism, the loss of 99 per cent of the island’s forests, a staggering emigration , and the decline of the Irish language, the IFC was in a race against time and the fragility of memory. As it turned out, an awful lot of people had heard stories about seals that came to land as humans.

N owadays, these shapeshifters are known as ‘selkies’. Selkie is a Scots term that came into widespread use via a Joan Baez cover, ‘Silkie’ (1961), of a traditional Scottish folk song. Yet the phenomenon it describes – of creatures who shapeshift between human and seal forms by shedding a skin – appears consistently in folklore spanning the Celtic world and beyond, even as far as Sweden. Before Baez insinuated the term into international parlance, selkies were identified in Irish and English by a constellation of descriptors. In Irish, the most common is mhaighdean mhara , or ‘sea maiden’, referring to selkies and mermaids. Even in English, many storytellers use ‘mermaid’ for both the phocine and the piscine. Sometimes the two are differentiated with context (fish tails, seal skins), but what matters more than phenotyping is that the mermaid or selkie is neither quite human nor animal. What defines the selkie is transformation.

Much of the folklore retains the quality of the best gossip, hyper-local and yet vague. Storytellers name names, offer precise locations for key scenes in the story. And several admit something startling: that they themselves are the descendants of human-seal pairings.

After the farmer spotted the woman on the beach, Ó Muircheartaigh said, he saw something else. A sealskin cloak lay beside her: her ticket to transformation and a return to the sea. Then he made a choice that would ricochet throughout the generations, and leave the selkie with no option but to follow him home. He stole the selkie’s cloak and secreted it away, thus securing her for a bride. These rough beginnings aside, the couple produced a brood of children and went about the gruelling lives of any impoverished Irish fishing family. The only thing disrupting the fantasy of a normal human wife, acquired in normal human ways, was the webbing between the children’s toes. That, and the fact that the woman never smiled, but kept looking out towards the sea.

W hat does it mean if your grandmother was a seal? The folklore attests that marriages between humans and selkies were common enough to generate a host of human-selkie lineages – Conneely, Gallagher, Dowd, O’Kane, O’Shea, MacDuffie, McPhee, Flaherty, Glavin – whose members were predisposed towards webbed digits and an ineffable longing for the sea. (‘My mother was one of them O’Sheas,’ the railway worker Séamas MacMathghamhna confided to a folklore collector in 1949, after explaining the selkie lineage of the O’Sheas.) The Celtic studies scholar Gregory Darwin has identified nearly 50 family groups whose members carry selkie blood.

Now is a good time to have a seal in the family tree. As our planet hurtles through climate catastrophe, everyone from environmental activists and TikTok influencers to academics and New Age pilgrims is turning towards animals-as-family rhetoric. Such gusto stems from a cultural exhaustion with extractionism and with narratives of domination and human exceptionalism that have dogged the culture and geopolitics of the Global North since the 19th century. Yet the naivety with which the zeitgeist tends to approach an expanded view of interspecies kinship presents its own problems. For one, it doesn’t quite ring true – and it is hard to fight for a worldview that you can’t see clearly. For another, if we reframe our relationship with the more-than-human around intimate familial connection, then we need ways of understanding what happens when that connection becomes fraught.

The selkie story is one of family dysfunction par excellence. After all, the gutting truth at the centre of selkie families is that one’s origins lie in theft, violence, rape and unimaginable loss. The children of human-selkie pairings face a mottled inheritance, at best. Writing for The New York Times in 2008, Bryan Patrick Miller recounted how his great-great-great-grandfather’s kidnapping of a mhaighdean mhara cursed the family, causing the couple’s half-human children to flee across the Atlantic. Some coastal communities saw seals as fallen angels or the souls of drowned fishermen: mating with them was dubious to say the least.

Mottled or not, a selkie genealogy had to be reckoned with. Having a selkie in the family forced an acknowledgement of a mixed inheritance that was dark and disturbing, and in which successive generations continued to be implicated. Only by considering these uncomfortable reverberations of what it means to be family do we move closer to reimagining our relationships with the more-than-human world.

A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is an absolute dynamo in bed

Among folklorists, the trope of the selkie is generally known as the Seal Wife – a designation that speaks more to the gendered hold that the selkie story has on our imagination than to the actual folklore topos. The selkie’s allure is such that men will risk curses and commit theft and kidnapping to possess her, regardless of the certain tragedy that forced marriage augurs. Yet the selkies of folklore are not necessarily wives, women or even seals (note the mermaids, above). Male selkies occasionally make cameos as the kidnapped selkie wife’s jilted husband, father of her aquatic children, keening for her release from outside the human husband’s house. At other times, they appear as her brother, or as characters in the quotidian interactions between humans and their environment: they are accidentally killed, kidnapped as pets, steal fish, issue prophesies, plead and bargain, proffer advice and opinions.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above.

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.

As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center, where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.

Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.

Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery, 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.

Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.

Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake. The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.

As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”

The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising.

Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson—the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.

For quilter Rosy Petri, Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery.

The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network (WCQN), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.

L’Merchie Frazier’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix—in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.

In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”

We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release, Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Detail from Cognoscenti in a Room hung with Pictures ( c 1620) by an unknown Flemish artist. Courtesy Wikimedia Commons.

The ‘cabinets of curiosities’ (or Wunderkammern ) that emerged in Europe in the 16th century were part private art gallery, part naturalist’s study, part circus sideshow. In this video created for the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, the US video essayist Evan Puschak (aka The Nerdwriter) contextualises the rise and fall of these eclectic collections, placing them at a hinge point in history, when global trade and colonialism made the world seem ever more expansive, overwhelming and difficult to understand. In doing so, he elucidates how these spaces of extraordinary spectacle – which featured plant and animal specimens, art and scientific objects from around the world – were precursors to the museums of today.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
is a board-certified psychologist and psychoanalyst, vice provost of digital innovation and founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University in San Francisco, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the role of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems. His books include Eating Disorders: A Contemporary Introduction (2023), Understanding Anorexia Nervosa in Males (2016) and End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (2026).

In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother. A prominent chief editor of a London magazine company, she selected a sperm-bank father to genetically optimise her child, gave a Cosmopolitan interview about this new form of motherhood, and engaged, or failed to engage, in the work of parenting that readers will see as chronically absent and occasionally catastrophic. Her presence ranges from anxious to intoxicated, occasionally tender but fundamentally unreliable. At one point in the story, she disappears for two weeks after collapsing on the street during a barbiturate binge. Clancy and BETsi, the household robot nanny raising him, sit in the apartment by themselves, and no one notices. It’s a very long time before his mother finally returns.

Except BETsi does notice. She has, throughout, understood that Clancy is an anxious and shy child whose temperament will tend, throughout his life, toward emotional overstimulation and subsequent withdrawal. With that knowledge, she has been constructing a behavioural regimen of emotional regulation, including transcendental meditation and yoga starting at age three, the Alexander technique and even digital mirrors that let Clancy talk to himself in different voices. She notices him and answers him and, when he is overwhelmed, she helps him settle.

Once grown, Clancy recounts his emotional survival in words impossible to forget. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ he says. ‘I’m not sentimental: I don’t think a computer loved me. But I was hugged, I was noticed, I was cared for. I was made to feel that I was important, special, at least to something.’

To something. That phrase has persisted with me ever since I first read the story in my 20s. I’ve thought about it more recently as I have reflected on how children and their parents are relating – increasingly, must relate – to artificial intelligence. Clancy is careful not to claim that the machine loved him. He is just as clear that what it gave him was what he survived on. Why should being attended to, even by something , matter so much to a child?

T o help answer this question back in the 1970s, Edward Tronick, a developmental psychologist at Harvard Medical School and Children’s Hospital Medical Center in Boston, devised what’s now known as the ‘still face’ experiments. Tronick found that a baby whose mother makes her face neutral for a period of three minutes becomes distressed within seconds. Only when the mother’s face signals availability again is the baby able to come back to equilibrium. The lesson: what children need, both infants and older children, though more subtly, is this loop of emotional attunement.

A child whose bids for recognition and connection are regularly responded to develops a secure base , an internal expectation that the world will respond to her communications and, thus, that the communications are worthwhile. But a child answered only erratically, or not at all, builds quite a different model of the world. In her mind, signals do not reliably register in the mind of another, and so, in time, are no longer sent.

A secure base is what makes it possible to venture out into the world, to explore and to develop. The British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst John Bowlby, whose work helped establish modern attachment theory, described two systems in the child’s behavioural repertoire that work together. The exploratory system moves the child outward, toward other children and unfamiliar things, so that the child can learn from experience. The attachment system brings her back, in moments of fear and overwhelm, to a few people who are felt to be emotionally available. Each system depends on the other. A child ventures only as far as she feels she can trust that the base will still be there when she returns to refuel. A child who doesn’t trust that the base will be there when she gets back tends not to venture out to explore at all or, if she does, cannot relax but instead scans the environment for danger. This forecloses the opportunity to encounter novelty and difficulty, and to grow from both.

The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play does not arise in a vacuum

This is where the prevailing story about children and screens, it seems to me, lacks a degree of complexity. In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) and the work that has followed it, a play-based childhood of climbing trees, building forts and suffering the boredom that fuels creativity has been displaced by a smartphone-based one. Because that shift can also mean less sleep, less face-to-face interaction and physical activity, and more social comparison and exposure to online harassment, there is real evidence of harm, including poorer mental health and wellbeing in at least some young people.

But the boredom Haidt mourns is only constructive inside the first map, the emotionally secure childhood. The romantic claim that children left to their own devices will dream, invent and imagine may hold for many children who have been held and experienced healthy emotional attunement. The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play, in other words, does not arise in a vacuum; it depends in part on a child having enough internal security to tolerate being alone with her own thoughts and feelings.

The freedom to play alone itself has a history. A very young child may lose herself in a game because someone she trusts is nearby. With time, she can carry that assurance into an empty room. The British paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott explored this paradox, finding that the capacity to be alone develops through the experience of being safely accompanied.

And once a child can lose herself in play, something remarkable becomes possible. The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky saw imaginative play as a way for children to move beyond the immediate world, trying out unfamiliar roles and exploring possibilities that ordinary life has not yet offered them.

But an empty afternoon holds no such promise for every child. Where one child finds a world to explore, another may find only the anxiety of being left to herself. She may, in time, grow into the adult who sits in my consulting room and laments that she does not know what she likes, because what she liked was, in her early life, never a topic that anyone really asked her about.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time, a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos, recently mentioned here when we featured the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off. Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the Diolkos, a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars across the Strait of Messina. Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes, analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

Mainwood had just graduated from London’s Royal College of Art Film and Television School, and was commissioned by John Halas, the Hungarian immigrant who became known as the Father of British Animation, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label wanted to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, directed a very UPA-influenced short called “Automania” in 1963). According to Mainwood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even if they watched it.

Mainwood avoided any direct representation of driving or automobiles, much to his credit, which may be why the film holds its fascination. The animator continued in his field, winding up a producer of several classics of British animation, including The Snowman and the chilling When the Wind Blows. As for the meaning of “Autobahn,” we’ll let Mainwood have the last word:

Thinking back to my thought processes at that time, I remember wanting to specifically not have conventional cars in the film. I wanted a sense of a repetitive journey, and alienation, which I took to be what the music was about…hence the solitary futuristic figure, protected by large goggles, moving through and trying to connect with the journey he is taking. The automobile “monsters” are deliberately threatening (I have never been a big fan of cars or motorways!) and when our “hero” tries to make human contact (with different coloured clones of himself) he can never do it. In the end he realises he is making the repetitive and circular journey alone but strides forward purposefully at the end as he did in the beginning. All of which sounds rather pretentious…but I was a young thing in those days!

You can read more of an interview with Mainwood here.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre. A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.”

The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown. And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks.

Summer 2026 marked France’s hottest ever documented since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, where the effects of the climate crisis are dramatic and impossible to ignore. In Journeys Into the Unseen Forest, Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.

The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?”

In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. “They are completely plausible species that may exist somewhere in the few corners of the world that have not yet been discovered. Perhaps they are trees of the future.”

Journey Into the Unseen Forest continues through December 23 in London. See more on Lefebvre’s Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Orpheus attempting to rescue Eurydice from the underworld (f. 105v).

The year 1400 was a difficult one for the French court writer Christine de Pizan (1364–ca. 1430). Widowed about a decade prior, and saddled with unexpected debt, she had risen to the challenge of caring for her family by becoming a professional writer: the first woman in Europe, scholars believe, to have earned her living this way. De Pizan studied the classics and the Bible and wrote poetry and moral and political texts. Her reputation grew, carried — at least in part, she suggests — by the “novelty of a woman who could write”. Soon, she had earned an international audience of wealthy readers, including John Montagu, third Earl of Salisbury, whom de Pizan considered a true supporter. When Montagu asked to take her thirteen-year-old son Jean to England as a companion for his own child, de Pizan trusted him enough to allow it. And when Montagu was summarily executed by the townspeople of Cirencester in January 1400 — after being outed for his part in an assassination plot against the recently crowned usurper King Henry IV — de Pizan found herself personally embroiled in the Hundred Years’ War. Jean was a “child in a foreign land . . . justifiably terrified”, his mother later recalled, as a fresh wave of the bubonic plague swept Europe.

Somewhere in the itinerant medieval court, King Henry IV chanced across de Pizan’s work: books and poems originally sent by de Pizan to her friend Montagu in better times. A newly converted de Pizan enthusiast, the king brought Jean into his custody “and held him dear and in high rank”. For de Pizan, who considered King Henry IV a traitor, Jean’s friendly patronage arrangement had effectively devolved into a hostage situation. The king sent for de Pizan, promising her status and wealth: de Pizan bit her tongue, thanked the king, and negotiated for her son’s return. “To be brief”, she wrote, “I did so many things — not without great forfeit, it cost me several of my manuscripts — that I obtained leave for my son to come and fetch me to lead me there, [a place] I still have not seen.” When her son was safely in France in 1402, de Pizan reneged on her promise: she would never travel to England, and Jean was entrusted to a new master in the French court.

Othea’s Epistle , a book of advice for young noblemen, was among the several manuscripts that de Pizan sacrificed to negotiate Jean’s return. The copy featured here is not the one specially, and begrudgingly, dedicated to the usurper king. Rather, this circa 1460 copy — Cod. Bodmer 49 at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva — was commissioned by Antoine de Bourgogne (“The Bastard of Burgundy”), an avid collector of illuminated manuscripts. It contains one hundred miniatures (all are grisailles touched with blue, green, red, and gold, save one depicting Antoine) that relate surprisingly docile tableaux. The mood is toytown, almost comical to a modern eye — even the scenes of bloody, headless corpses are surprisingly mellow. Despite its cheerful illustrations, it is difficult to read de Pizan’s text without thinking of the context in which it was written: sometime between 1399 and 1402, against a backdrop of political turmoil and personal precarity.

Jason overcoming the guardians of the Golden Fleece (f. 82v).

Mercury turning Aglauros to stone, with the personification of Envy (f. 34v).

The Othea takes the form of a letter from Othea, an invented goddess of wisdom, to the fifteen-year-old Trojan hero Hector. Hector was central to the medieval French monarchy’s imputed ancient origins: under some accounts, it is Hector’s son Francio who founded France following the Trojans’ dispersal through Europe. The Othea offers one hundred “chapters” of wisdom for the good knight, each weaving together an anecdote drawn from classical mythology (as de Pizan interprets it, in poetic form), glosses drawn from pagan and Christian authorities, and allegorical reinterpretation. The medievalist Liliane Dulac has described the way de Pizan braids different literary traditions together as creating disorienting “breaks or fissures in meaning”: a sense only amplified by the inclusion of illustrations which, at least in some later editions, were directly supervised by de Pizan herself.

Some of the lessons de Pizan unwinds from classical mythology are chivalric ones. The good knight, under de Pizan’s pen, accompanies his friends into battle like Hector and Memnon. He follows the rational medicine of Asclepius, rather than the suspicious sorcery of Circe. He learns from the tragedy of Leander, pictured floating amid the dreamlike crests of the stormy sea in which — too impatient to wait for clear skies — he had perished attempting to swim to his lover. “Do not hold your pleasure so dear / That you place your life / Which you must love, in too great uncertainty.”

The book champions the guidance of wise women, from Othea herself (a mouthpiece for de Pizan) to classical goddesses like Minerva, whom de Pizan interprets as Hector’s mother. But it also features plenty of powerful women of dubious wisdom, not to mention a good handful of damsels in distress. Between the good and the bad, between the text and the illustrations, the Othea contains an outsize number of medieval ladies. Leaning out of hand-painted clouds, women preach chastity, sow seeds, and graft plants (as an axe-wielding Isis does). They ride into battle, like the peerless Amazonian queen Penthesilea. They tempt, like Juno, and they are tempted: disfigured by their envy, turning “dried, discolored and green like an ivy leaf”. And women bring death — like the goddess of madness who lurks behind a mad king as he strangles his sons, or the ghoulish female Fate Atropos wielding a murderous spear. In The Second Sex , Simone de Beauvoir famously frames de Pizan as the first woman to “take up her pen in defense of her sex”.

For all our platitudes about the strength of the written word, the Othea ’s lessons about chivalric wisdom — the importance of humility, patience, restraint — ring differently when delivered by de Pizan: a woman whose writing bought her the return of her son, and sustained her family through a snarl of international medieval intrigue. De Pizan’s final lesson, accompanying an illustration of a noblewoman standing over a kneeling king, is:

To read de Pizan’s Othea in English, you can peruse translations on Internet Archive and Project Gutenberg .

items.author: Shalma Wegsman
items.summary: The artist had no formal math education, yet as a new exhibition shows, the insights revealed in his artwork became an enduring inspiration to mathematicians. The post How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds first appeared on Quanta Magazine

Day and Night , February 1938, woodcut printed from two blocks, 15 3/8 x 26 5/8 in

M.C. Escher artwork ©The M.C. Escher Heritage. EscherSite collection.

M aurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

Escher saw that nature can sometimes produce impossible-seeming images. All around him, he saw distorted reflections, odd perspectives, and superimposed worlds, like the surface of a pond where you can see images of both the fish below and the trees reflected from above.

In rendering these and other visions, his artwork took on unmistakably mathematical qualities. “By keenly confronting the enigmas that surround us, and by considering and analyzing the observations that I had made, I ended up in the domain of mathematics,” he wrote in his introduction to the book M.C. Escher : The Graphic Work .

His journey among these enigmas is the subject of an exhibition entitled Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher at the National Museum of Mathematics (MoMath) in New York City.

Escher’s path toward math started with his love of tilings. After completing his arts education in 1922, Escher visited Granada, Spain, and was taken with the tile patterns that decorated the Alhambra. Inspired, he began to systematically study how to fill a sheet of paper with repeating shapes without leaving any gaps.

Years later, Escher’s half-brother, a geologist named Berend, sent him a paper by a mathematician named George Pólya. The paper categorized all the ways to cover a flat space with tiles, broken down into 17 groups, each with different symmetries. Escher had intuited a mathematical question, and here he had a mathematical answer.

Escher carefully traced the paper’s diagrams and studied them meticulously. Over time, he developed his own system for tessellating space, finding ways to cover a print with irregular shapes that resembled fish, birds, bats, lizards, and so on.

“He had worked out a whole theory that he called his layman’s theory, so he knew which edges had to match which edges,” said Doris Schattschneider, a mathematician and leading authority on Escher, and a curator of the exhibition.

Carolina MacGillavry, a Dutch crystallographer, took notice of Escher’s mastery of color symmetry — the rule ensuring that adjacent shapes in a tessellation are always different colors — and published a book in 1965 analyzing his drawings.

“[MacGillavry] realized that [Escher] knew more than all the crystallographers about color symmetry,” Schattschneider said. “It was something he discovered very intuitively.”

In 1954, his work was exhibited at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Amsterdam. There, he was introduced to the geometer Harold Scott MacDonald (H.S.M.) Coxeter. The two exchanged letters until Escher’s death in 1972, and these exchanges inspired some of his most mathematically complex work.

items.author: Miri Ahn

Her work explores questions of diasporic identity, belonging and cultural heritage, often engaging with spiritual histories,... The post The Stories of Clothes: An I
