Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Zadie Xa is a London-based multidisciplinary artist from Vancouver, Canada, whose practice spans painting, textiles, sound, installation, and performance. Her work explores questions of diasporic identity, belonging and cultural heritage, often engaging with spiritual histories, and folklore.

For the second iteration of New Work: The Stories of Clothes at V&A East Museum, Xa presents Amulets, a textile installation of seven jackets that gradually transform in scale and form. Inspired by traditional ceremonial garments and contemporary streetwear, the commission explores how clothing can communicate identity, and embody power.

Can you briefly describe your practice and the questions or ideas that guide your work?

In my practice I am interested in exploring ideas of placehood, belonging and identity through interspecies relations, spiritual histories, and the preservation and evolution of folk traditions.

How did you come to work this way? What are particular moments, influences or experiences that shaped your vision?

I studied painting during both my undergraduate and master’s degrees, but eventually moved beyond conventional painting to engage directly with the materials and forms I had been referencing, like music and clothing. This led me to experiment with live performance and later with installation.

The transition from painting to a multidisciplinary practice came naturally to me. My approach to texture, colour and materials has been shaped by rifling through racks of clothing and shelves of knick-knacks in vintage shops as a teenager, as well as by my interest in music and sampling.

Rather than representing these influences solely through painting, I began incorporating them directly into my work. This has led me towards a more expansive way of working, opening up my practice to new materials and disciplines.

I am also deeply inspired by traditional clothing from around the world. I especially love the stories communities share through their regalia. This is also why I find music, and particularly sampling culture within hip-hop and pop music, so interesting.

Across disciplines, I use references to convey political ideas, pay homage and explore what emerges when contemporary forms meet historical traditions. This mixing relates to my own interest in hybridity and third-culture identities.

The commission is a textile installation comprising seven jackets suspended in a row, as if in procession. Each garment increases in scale from the first to the seventh, with the jackets connected as though growing and shapeshifting from one form or style into another.

How did you begin developing this work? What was your starting point?

My starting point was a site visit to V&A East, where I encountered a striking Daoist robe that became a key reference point.

I have long been interested in religious, spiritual and traditional regalia, particularly how their construction and printed or embroidered imagery communicate the wearer’s identity, local history, beliefs and political status.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In summer 2025, Sian Fan was selected as a Design Trust Fellow at V&A East . Her proposed project was to travel for the first time to Hong Kong and the New Territories to trace her Hakka family history and to search through the V&A’s collection for objects relating to her heritage.

As an artist as well as a contemporary and aerial dancer, Sian creates sculpture, costume, performance, animation, installation, and new media which is often informed by her questioning of her mixed Hakka Chinese and British identity.

Here Sian shares with us tales of her field research and the making of her new commission, The Body is a Relic (how the light gets in) , which is on show in Gallery 3 of V&A East Storehouse.

Can you describe how your research began at V&A East Storehouse?

My research involved attempting to trace my familial journey as a Hakka descendant. As with many migrant stories it is punctured with gaps, holes and voids and I wanted to use the research to reframe these absences as opportunities for the creation of speculative stories.

Considering how in my and in many migrant families there is an absence of heirlooms and of tangible objects that connect with one’s family history, I wanted to embrace the V&A collections as a huge archive of proxy heirlooms. I was particularly inspired by the Liangmao hat as well as by Hakka textiles which are incredibly resourceful and make careful and attentive use of scraps of available fabrics. I’ve also taken inspiration from the Chinese embroidery within the collection.

And how was your field research in Hong Kong and the New Territories of Hong Kong and Fujian?

For my field research I visited Hong Kong and China for the first time. I spent time exploring the cityscape of Hong Kong, being immersed in the hectic and humid streets and visiting the different art organisations based there. I also visited heritage museums where I learnt about the cultural traditions of Hong Kong and Hakka people. In the New Territories of Hong Kong, I visited a friend’s Hakka village and attended a celebration for the re-opening of the village temple where there were lion dances, firecrackers and poon choi. I also hiked through rural New Territories to Kop Tong, my family’s ancestral village and found the abandoned house that my mum grew up in, before she left Hong Kong for England as a child.

Here I was able to glimpse and attempt to piece together her fragments of memories from her time there and it was a powerful and surreal experience. I discovered a small museum in the nearby Lai Chi Wo village that had information on the area that included information on my family as well as reconstructions of a Hakka style home, which jogged some of my mum’s memories when I later showed them to her. In Fujian I visited several Toulou buildings, which are a traditional form of Hakka architecture, which are usually circular structures with an open courtyard in the centre.

Can you describe your commission for V&A East Storehouse?

The commission is called The Body is a Relic (how the light gets in) . It is an installation consisting of three suspended body-like, life-sized sculptures representing a small family unit. The bodies have rounded bamboo frames, which are covered in different textured fabrics with differing opacities. Their heads appear as if wrapped in branches or vines, and the space where the head and neck would be is a cut-out, negative space. Strung vertically inside each body is a glowing light bar, which shines through the differing materials, revealing shapes within the layers, making the bodies akin to lanterns.

The textured materials feature images captured over the research trip rendered via embroidery and weaving. These images range from cut out wall features from traditional Hakka architecture, the patterned glass windowpane of my mother’s childhood home, the ornamental koi within one of the toulous and the lion dancers from the village celebrations. These are layered, distorted and reconfigured to create an abstract tapestry that reimagines memories, histories and stories.

The bamboo structures reference Hong Kong’s famous bamboo scaffold and the branch like structure of the figures’ heads is inspired by the winding branches that I encountered hiking to my ancestral village. The negative space of the body references the oculus like voids within the toulou houses and the opening for the head in the lian mao hats. In both of these examples, the empty space is filled with the body, filled with life.

Conceptually the work meditates upon disjointed histories and speculative story making, weaving together tales both real and imagined with equal value as a method of asserting agency over one’s historic and cultural identity, enabling a sense of belonging and dreaming into reality new states of self. The work explores how in the absence of heirlooms, tangible histories and family stories that the body is a tangible and meaningful record: the body itself is a relic.

items.author: Miri Ahn
items.summary: R.I.P. Germain is a LA-based multidisciplinary artist born in Luton. His practice examines Black experience, identity and cultural history For the second iteration of New Work, The Stories of Clothes, Germain draws on his experience... The post The Stories of Clothes: An Interview with R.I.P. Germain appeared first on

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
R.I.P. Germain is a LA-based multidisciplinary artist born in Luton. His practice examines Black experience, identity and cultural history

For the second iteration of New Work , The Stories of Clothes , Germain draws on his experience of moving from the UK to Los Angeles and becoming more acutely aware of the highly specific meanings attached to clothing in different parts of the city. As a large Black man, he recognises that particular colours, brands or styles could lead others to associate him with a local gang, potentially placing him in danger. Clothing therefore became more than a form of personal expression. It operated as a social code through which identity, affiliation and threat could be read or misread.

Can you briefly describe your practice and the questions or ideas that guide your work?

Unruly fukkry. That’s where my head’s at right now with my practice. I’m really enjoying creating with this mindstate. It’s liberating. I’m not concerned with whether the works I’m making are gallery friendly or institutional…at all. To meet me, think of it like this, there are five questions that I cycle through constantly during the process of making a work. They sort of act like five pendants hung on my chain (practice).

These questions have become a mantra – they keep me focused, and on the right path. Rigid and fluid.

How did you come to work this way? What are particular moments, influences or experiences that shaped your vision?

‘Brixton Quincey talks doing Black Magic (Juju) & Shoot out (Part 5) #OFTR’ – LSL FILMS

‘good kid, m.A.A.d city – A Short Film by Kendrick Lamar’ – Kendrick Lamar

In that order. That’ll give you a little bit of insight into where I’ve come from.

wheeloffortune is a horror agent. It is art imitating aspects of my life and riffing off of it. The film consists of a slideshow of polaroids of individual items of clothing as well as configurations of said clothes, that can be and have been used as signals of kinship, as well as acts of war in Los Angeles, depending on where you find yourself in the city, and if you’re Black or Brown. Aesthetic languages from the high end luxury streetwear industry, African American Angeleno gangbanging culture, and crime scene forensics are interwoven to visualise a long period of ponderment from myself about trying to come to terms with being a walking target, being seen as a threat, being considered a threat and being treated as a threat. You might think those last three things are similar, but they are not! The threat of danger is completely different between the three. wheeloffortune is not meant to have answers for the questions I’m posing with it, it is a very much needed act of respite, and a peek through another lens into the absurdities of modern Americana and the constant hum of terror that it manages to impose on the people that live in the US.

How did you begin developing this work? What was your starting point?

A near death experience. It sprouts from there. It’s one of two byproducts of a clarity of thought from a period of reflection.

What was your process like for researching and making this commission?

I wouldn’t even attempt to try to figure out how many hours I spent sourcing the clothes that were used in wheeloffortune . I remember it taking me five months of consistent searching on the internet in secondary clothing marketplaces to find one fitted hat. Every piece of clothing in the film is either something an African American gangbanger in Los Angeles would actually wear to show their affiliation to their gang, or it features a reference and/or symbol that with artistic licence on my part, could be worn by a gang member to show their allegiance to a specific gang. One example of that artistic licence being used would be that the yellow pieces of clothing that feature in the film are meant to result in an outfit that a member of the Main Street Mafia Crips could wear. So, because they wear clothes that typically sport an “M” logo on them of some kind, and the clothes are either blue, yellow or both in colour, such as the Michigan Wolverines fitted cap, I bought a quite rare collaborative hoodie between Palace and McDonalds, and a pair of Evisu Daicock Print #2000 Baggy-Fit Jeans, because they both have a yellow “M” looking logo blasted on them. This attention to detail has been applied to every item of clothing. There is some type of lore attached to all of them, whether that be through the difficulty in me acquiring them and/or the history attached to the item of clothing itself in relation to the fashion world.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Industrial Designers Jimin Jeon and Adam Huxley Khng have been working together since they met in Tokyo in 2019. The duo were selected as inaugural Design Trust Fellows in 2025. They have been researching garment fasteners within the V&A’s collection as well as in Hong Kong and China.

Here Adam and Jimin share with us their research journey and how they developed their final commissioned installation on display in Gallery 1 of V&A East Storehouse: Motions and Notions of Fastening.

Can you describe the research you conducted as part of the Design Trust Fellowship?

Adam: Our research focused on garment fastenings and the recurring gestures and forms associated with them. We became interested in the actions and principles that have accompanied fastening technologies from prehistory to the present day, and the ways those forms have evolved through continuous refinement and adaptation.

We started with the idea that fastenings are much more than functional mechanisms or decorative details. They fundamentally shape the architecture and construction of clothing. Drawing on our background in industrial design, we became interested in understanding how fastenings have been conceived, developed and manufactured over time, and how they might continue to evolve in the future.

Jimin: One idea that became particularly important to us was what we described as an investigative process. When you encounter a museum object, you are often given information such as its materials, dimensions or date, but there is so much that remains unknown. You don’t necessarily know how it was used, how it felt to handle, or what role it played in everyday life. That absence of information becomes productive. It invites speculation and reflection.

Jimin: The ability to handle objects during our research time at the V&A East Storehouse was incredibly important. For example, when we examined a jade belt hook, the catalogue could tell us what it was and roughly when it was made, but it couldn’t communicate the experience of holding it. The moment you pick it up, you feel its weight. You notice the temperature of the jade. You hear the subtle sound made when the pieces connect. Those qualities don’t exist in photographs or catalogue records. They can only be understood through direct experience. That kind of encounter became one of the most valuable parts of the project.

How did the opportunity to research in Hong Kong, China and the Greater Bay Area influence your practice?

Adam: The trip gave us a much broader understanding of production. We weren’t just interested in individual products; we wanted to understand the entire journey of an object, from manufacture and distribution through to sale and use. One of the most striking experiences was visiting manufacturing centres where huge quantities of fastenings are produced. You start to see how a seemingly small component can have enormous significance within a local economy and a much wider global network.

Jimin: Meeting people was equally important. There was a remarkable sense of immediacy and openness. Someone would say, “Do you want to see this?” and suddenly you were being introduced to another manufacturer or another part of the production process. Trust and personal connections played a significant role in how knowledge and expertise moved through the industry.

Adam: When we began the project, we expected to discover dramatic technological change. We found that, of course. But what surprised us was how much had remained the same. Many of the fundamental principles of fastening have changed very little over thousands of years. What has changed are the methods of production, the contexts in which objects operate, and the networks through which they circulate. That continuity between past and present became one of the most important discoveries of the project.

How did you approach classifying the garment fasteners you were researching?

Jimin: Instead of categorising fastenings according to their appearance or historical period, we started classifying them according to action and movement. Gradually, three primary categories emerged.

The first was piercing : materials joined through penetration, such as pins, brooches or other forms that hold materials together by passing through them.

items.author: Miri Ahn
items.summary: East London Textile Arts (ELTA) is a Newham-based, artist-led community textile collective that has been working with local communities since 2007. Bringing together people of different ages, backgrounds and abilities, ELTA creates ambitious collaborative textile... The post The Stories of Clothes: An Interview with Ea

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
East London Textile Arts (ELTA) is a Newham-based, artist-led community textile collective that has been working with local communities since 2007. Bringing together people of different ages, backgrounds and abilities, ELTA creates ambitious collaborative textile projects rooted in long-term relationships, shared creativity and the belief that art should be accessible to everyone.

Since the early development of V&A East, ELTA has been a collective we have wanted to work with. Its longstanding commitment to Newham’s communities, and its approach to textiles as a way of expressing personal and collective experiences, resonate closely with V&A East’s ambitions.

For the second iteration of New Work: The Stories of Clothes , ELTA has created a new installation exploring what people love and fear. Developed with members of the collective and local community groups, the commission brings together embroidered garments, photography and a large circular patchwork skirt, transforming a public space into a celebration of collective creativity and the stories that clothes can tell.

We spoke with Celia and Sonia, who lead ELTA, about their practice, creative process, and the experiences behind this new commission.

Can you briefly describe your practice and the ideas that guide your work?

Celia: ELTA’s members are ethnically diverse, mostly women, older and on low incomes. Many have health conditions or disabilities, and many speak English as an additional language. Over 25% of the collective have learning disabilities, with members ranging in age from their 20s to their early 60s.

We believe that high-quality textiles can be made within non-professional communities that have a long-term vision. ELTA works collectively and focuses on building lasting creative relationships with communities in Newham, rather than treating each project as a separate, one-off activity.

How did you come to work this way? What are particular moments, influences or experiences that shape your vision?

Celia: I came to work this way after spending three years in Bucharest, Romania, where I was greatly influenced by the Muzeul Naţional al Ţăranului Român (National Museum of the Romanian Peasant) and its director during the 1990s, Horia Bernea, who redesigned the museum after the collapse of communism.

He transformed it into a space that focused on craftwork made by people as part of their daily lives, work not generally thought of as ‘art’. The museum’s design, with its hand-painted walls and refusal to give space to marketing posters, gave it a unity and purpose: to celebrate the gifts and lives of Romanian people. I was also inspired by its political purpose, to reconsider what it meant to be human in a post-communist world.

Other influences include non-professional ‘village’ textiles, such as those of the Rabari communities in Gujarat, Romanian village textiles, and various textile NGOs established in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh to develop and sell embroidery and other handcrafted textiles.

When I arrived in Newham from Romania in 2005, I was struck by the vibrant colours of the many Asian textile shops, the different festivals and street processions. Everywhere there were the most colourful and varied textiles and clothes. It made me want to drop painting and join this party of cloth.

Sonia: I met Celia in 2007 and, having an interest in embroidery, I joined the project. I went on to teach and design with groups, collaborating with Celia on project development.

Celia: Our commission for the V&A is a wall installation comprising 9 kaftans, one quilt, one scarf, thirteen photographs and one crazy patchwork hanging/skirt.

Her practice is eclectic – moving between photography, textile, sculpture, video and... The post The Stories of Clothes: An interview with Alia Ali appeared first on V&A Blog .

Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Arist Alia Ali works with light, language and architecture, as these are the tools she sees us understand and construct worlds around us. Her practice is eclectic – moving between photography, textile, sculpture, video and installation work – and often works across borders, travelling for her artworks to the source of materials and craft skills she wants to explore.

In 2025, Ali joined the V&A as the Jameel Fellow and investigated objects in the collection which attested to the material culture of the Indian Ocean world with her home-country of Yemen at its centre. Her research informed her newly commissioned installation at the V&A East Museum, Portable Sanctuaries: 3000 years ago/Now/3000 years forward . Here Ali shares with us her insights into the V&A’s collection and why and how her new commission was created.

‘Hand and Land’ are two guiding principles for your work – can you explain this?

There is the land: plants, animals, minerals, water, soil, metals, stones. And there is the hand. Between them exist centuries, sometimes millennia, of knowledge.

I am less interested in asking someone, “Where are you from?” because I am not sure geography alone can answer that question. I am more interested in asking: What do your hands make? What land has sustained you? What do you wear? What do you carry? What have you inherited? What protects you? What travels with you even when it cannot be seen?

These are also the questions I take into my research with objects. For example, cloth is never simply decorative. It carries histories of movement, trade, colonisation, labour, belief and exchange. It can travel enormous distances while retaining evidence of everywhere it has been. A pattern can migrate. A dye can migrate. A technique can migrate. A word can migrate. A person can migrate. None necessarily arrives unchanged, but neither does it entirely leave behind where it came from. But cloth is also extraordinarily intimate. We wrap ourselves in it. We sleep in it. We protect ourselves with it. We inherit it. We carry it when we move.

What was the starting point for your research as part of the Jameel Fellowship?

I wanted to understand Yemen through its millennia-long participation in the Indian Ocean world, and through the histories of the places with which it has exchanged ideas, materials, people, language and belief: India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia, what is now Singapore, Zanzibar, Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia, Oman and many others. Yemen begins to look very different when it is understood through water rather than through continental borders. It is so often imagined externally through desert and land, but I relate to Yemen very strongly through water and mountains. Its history is profoundly maritime. I began thinking about Yemen as something much more Afro–Indo–Arab than what can be contained within a purely continental understanding of West Asia or the Middle East.

I spent three months working within the V&A’s Asia Department, guided particularly by Rachel Dedman, Jameel Curator of Contemporary Art from the Middle East, and in conversation with curators working across different parts of Asia and different material histories, including fashion and textiles. I also spent an extraordinary amount of time in V&A East Storehouse, in the stacks and collections, simply looking, guided by Georgia Haseldine, Senior Curator, V&A East Storehouse. Alongside this, through the V&A’s Cultures in Crisis programme with Laura Searson, I began exploring conflict as a starting point rather than an endpoint: how to break from the dystopic narratives that so often surround places marked by conflict, and instead look through the past, including the nostalgia we attach to it, as a way of giving space to reimagined futures.

I was drawn to objects that sat somewhere between beauty, belief, danger, protection, adornment and the body. They came from very different times, geographies and material worlds, and many of them would probably never ordinarily be placed beside one another. What became interesting to me was allowing those objects to speak across those distances. An ancient talismanic garment could sit in my mind alongside a contemporary dress. An object made to carry something close to the body could speak to an object intended to protect it. Creatures, language, minerals, textiles and forms began to create relationships that were not necessarily there when I first encountered them.

Some of these objects I’ve put together into a display at V&A East Storehouse.

The fellowship fundamentally changed my relationship to geography and time. Looking deeply at objects from the past made me realise that I wasn’t particularly interested in history simply as something to recover or look back upon. It became material through which I could look forward.

I began thinking about approximately 3,000 years behind us and imagining 3,000 years ahead. If these languages, materials, stories, creatures, symbols, plants, minerals and relationships have travelled thousands of years to reach us, then I want the work to insist upon their right to continue travelling. To me, that insistence is radical.

The future does not have to mean abandoning the earth or the knowledge that brought us here. It doesn’t have to mean colonising the constellations. Perhaps imagining the future requires us to understand more deeply what has already sustained us.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The Argentine physicist Gabriel Mindlin has spent much of his career researching how birds learn to sing. He focuses on the rufous-collared sparrow ( Zonotrichia capensis ), a species common across urban and suburban Argentina, where it’s often called a ‘chingolo’. As in other songbirds, the male’s song is not innate but passed down from adult males to younger ones, who sing it throughout their lives to guard territory and find a mate.

In this short documentary, the Argentine director Martín Benchimol chronicles Mindlin’s latest breakthrough. Comparing the songs of today’s chingolos with those transcribed by hand in the 1960s, Mindlin realised that some melodies had survived the decades while others had disappeared. Using mathematical models, he and his team set out to revive the vanished songs and teach them back to living birds. With a cinematic eye, Benchimol follows the researchers as they attempt an audacious act of cultural engineering, building robotic song tutors, planting them in the wild and tracking whether young birds pick up these lost tunes.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Generations of Westerners have come to appreciate Japanese cinema through the films of Akira Kurosawa, but many have been shocked to find out that Kurosawa himself isn’t as beloved in Japan as they’d imagined. It’s less that his homeland rejects him than that his work has been regarded there as a somewhat foreign taste. That judgment must have something to it: despite their thoroughly Japanese settings, Throne of Blood, The Bad Sleep Well, and Ran were, after all, Shakespeare adaptations, and Kurosawa spoke openly of structuring his stories in the manner of not just traditional Japanese theater, but also symphonies. Consider, too, the way his films continue to inspire Western remakes, from The Magnificent Seven and A Fistful of Dollars in the nineteen-sixties to Living and Highest 2 Lowest in this decade.

Nor can it be a coincidence that the appreciative voices opening the StudioBinder video on Kurosawa’s genius above belong to Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, and George Lucas. Yet this most internationally celebrated of all Japanese filmmakers can’t, ultimately, have been just a Westerner in disguise, since his work gives viewers around the world something that their domestic movies don’t.

Whatever the extent to which he hybridized the cinematic sensibilities of Japan and Hollywood, he did so through his uncompromising personal involvement in every stage of the process. “The role of the director encompasses the coaching of the actors, the cinematography, the sound recording, the art direction, the music, the editing, and the dubbing and sound mixing,” he once said, expressing his dedication to the ideal of (as no less an American auteur than Jerry Lewis described himself) the total filmmaker.

That Kurosawa understood how to tell a story in a way that transcends cultural boundaries goes without saying; what’s less widely appreciated is the way he did so with a combination of simplicity and complexity. As he put it, “a truly good movie is interesting and easy to understand,” two qualities that often end up in irresolvable tension, at least in the hands of lesser filmmakers. Even among those influenced by Kurosawa, for example, some have mastered immediate visual legibility without ever understanding that sound and music are more effectively used as a counterpoint to, rather than mere intensification of, a scene’s prevailing emotion. How many living directors, for that matter, convincingly approach grand, universal themes without irony or protective distance? If Kurosawa’s films retain a power that seems inaccessible today, it may be because, for him, there was no East or West: there was only cinema.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Earlier this month, Salon announced that it’s ceasing publication after 31 years. In its farewell address, the magazine writes: “The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable.” We can sympathize.

Over the 20 years we have served you, we have watched quality websites come and go. Some once-vibrant sites have gone entirely dark. Today, if you want to sift through the remains of the early internet, you can head over to the Internet Archive—a site that “captures and stores over one trillion web pages to safeguard digital history and prevent the rewriting or erasure of online records.” In the case of Salon, the Internet Archive has launched Salon Explorer, a “new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism.” According to a new blog post from the Internet Archive, the tool lets you browse more than 250,000 articles and explore the work of over 20,000 writers, with filters that make it easier to find stories you may have missed. If it isn’t your preferred interface, you can also browse Salon.com using the Wayback Machine. RIP Salon, long live the Internet Archive.

Enter the Salon Explorer here.

If you would like to support the mission of Open Culture, consider making a donation to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your contributions will help us continue providing the best free cultural and educational materials to learners everywhere. items.summary: Women in Tehran are changing society by dressing as they choose, in numbers too large to stop. This is the ‘art of presence’ - by Parisa Khoshnami Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
At a café in downtown Tehran, Iran, on 11 September 2026. Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/via Getty Images

is an Iranian writer who lives in Paris, France. Her work has appeared in The New Statesman , BBC Persian, Euronews Persian as well as in Iranian journals.

Yasaman* is one of the regulars on Iranshahr, the new fashion hub of Tehran. Most evenings, she sets up a stall on the pavement and sells her drawings of manga and anime characters. On social media, she sports her own manga-inspired look: pink hair, pink mouth and smudgy pink eyeshadow extending beyond the corner of each eye. She tells her followers that, before she leaves her house, her mother says: ‘Put on less makeup.’ ‘Mum, be reasonable,’ she answers. ‘I’m going to Iranshahr. For Iranshahr this is nothing. I’m going to Paris Fashion Week. You know everyone there is doing a catwalk.’

Iranshahr’s sidewalks teem with young people parading the latest fashions and filming other young, stylish people for their social media feeds. This is where the fashionistas congregate, hanging out in cafés and galleries, and mingling on the sidewalks. Barely a headscarf is visible. The streets looked nothing like this a few years ago, but once the American-Israeli attacks began in February this year, the Islamic Republic has been fighting for its survival: with much of its leadership killed, the Strait of Hormuz under siege, and many of the country’s neighbours in league with the enemy, policing what people wear has slipped a long way down its list of priorities.

The hijab law has been codified in Iran since 1983, enforced nationwide by the ‘morality’ police. Disobeying it meant fines, flogging or imprisonment. But then one act of disobedience changed everything. In December 2017, Vida Movahed, a woman in her 30s, climbed onto a utility box on Enghelab Street in Tehran, took off her white headscarf and held it up on a stick. Although she was arrested and later sentenced to a year in prison, her action proved contagious. Other women climbed up onto boxes and makeshift plinths in the same street, waving their headscarves in the air. People began calling them the Girls of Enghelab Street. They were arrested too. It is hard to convey now how much nerve their actions took. Women had been edging their scarves back for years, but taking one off in daylight, above the traffic, where the police could see their naked heads as clearly as everyone else, was something very few women had done in public, since the protests of 1979 and 1980.

Then, in September 2022, Mahsa Jina Amini died in custody of the morality police. Unlike the women on the boxes, she was not an activist: aged 22, a Kurdish woman visiting from Saqqez, a city 600 km west of Tehran, she’d been stopped because her loose headscarf was not covering enough of her hair. Her death brought thousands of people out on to the street in an outpouring of grief and anger. Women burned their headscarves. Cut their hair in front of cameras. Their protests spawned the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, and continued for months. What began as a demand for justice for one woman became a challenge to the compulsory hijab, then to the system itself. The authorities responded with arrests, executions and a repression that has never really stopped. The funerals of the dead became protests in their turn.

W hat changed was that the morality police largely disappeared from the streets for months afterwards, with no announcement that the patrols had ended. Women who had grown up expecting to be stopped were not being stopped, and they knew why: the government had learned in 2022 what a single arrest could cost.

Azadeh, a woman from Tehran, tells me that, during the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, the city felt apocalyptic. After the US president Donald Trump posted that people in Tehran should get out of the city, they fled their homes, leaving everything behind, and the city emptied. Checkpoints multiplied as the government waited for an uprising that never came. But in the strange mood that settled on the city following the attacks, Azadeh noticed another change – a bargain that nobody signed: ‘The state began leaving people alone to live as they like, as long as they do not come out into the street about it.’

‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together’

What is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules that have governed daily life for decades. A few inches of visible hair used to be the whole argument, but it is no longer the point. Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. Enjoying this new freedom, they parade along Iranshahr (rather aptly, the street takes its name from the old Persian word for the land of the Iranians), where shops that used to sell manteaus and headscarves have switched to blouses and T-shirts.

A young woman whom I’ll call Mina puts the shift in blunter terms. ‘It isn’t optional anymore,’ she said. ‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together.’ She does not wear a headscarf anymore, and nor does anyone she goes out with. On the streets where people go to be seen, she tells me, hardly anyone does. In Tehran, those who can afford it wear the latest designer clothing. But in small Iranian towns, local workshops turn out such good copies of the latest Parisian and New York trends that anyone can now dress head to toe in ‘Chanel’, whatever their class.

Sima, also from Tehran, says that: ‘Among the women who dress freely there is a kind of solidarity. Nobody talks about it, but everyone feels it.’ Recalling the first time she removed her headscarf, Sima says: ‘I felt bald … I thought everyone was looking at me, and I kept checking.’ She was frightened, she told me, so she kept a headscarf in her bag ready to whip out if anything should happen. It took a while for the feeling to pass. Each time she went out, she saw more women without headscarves and that gave her heart. She knew that she was not alone.

T he easy read on these developments, especially outside Iran, is that this is defiance: using clothing as a weapon against the state. The framing is not entirely wrong, but it misses most of what is happening on the street, and the people living it do not describe what they are up to in this way. When I asked Mina if getting dressed felt like a political act, she paused, then said no. ‘When I dress up, it’s only for myself,’ she told me. ‘I’m not doing some political act.’ So what is happening on Iranshahr?

The Iranian sociologist Asef Bayat has spent years asking how ordinary people can change their societies in the absence of formal organisations or conventional political movements. In Life as Politics: How Ordinary People Change the Middle East (2010), he argues that they do it less by protesting than by simply living as they wish to, and in enough numbers and for long enough that the rules have to bend around them. Bayat’s name for what Sima, Mina and Azadeh are describing is ‘the art of presence’. It denotes ‘the courage and creativity to assert collective will in spite of all odds, to circumvent constraints, utilising what is available and discovering new spaces within which to make oneself heard, seen, felt, and realised.’ It is a form of soft power.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“La ciudad es más que la gente.” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to Invasión’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters Adolfo Bioy Casares. Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled Borges) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own ficciones, it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that Invasión was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in one version with optional English and French subtitles, and another, higher resolution version with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding foley work and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, Nouvelle Vague, political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about Invasión, there is no one answer.

items.title: What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing.
items.author: Charlie Wood
items.summary: An era-defining galaxy survey has released its final results. They don’t quite fit the leading theory of cosmology. The post What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing. first appeared on Quanta Magazine

The 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera is mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope on Cerro Tololo near La Serena, Chile.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/ DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

J oshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to plan a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then, in early 1998, two teams of researchers announced that exploding stars called supernovas seemed to be racing away from Earth under the influence of an unidentified, omnipresent repellent force. The observations implied the existence of exactly the sort of missing energy that Frieman and his colleagues planned to talk about.

“Suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop,” including reporters with TV cameras, said Frieman, who was then at the University of Chicago. It was “kind of a circus.”

Within a few years, cosmologists had arrived at a whole new view of reality. The missing energy, given the name “dark energy” for its invisible nature, was pushing galaxies apart. The energy seemed embedded in space itself. It made up roughly two-thirds of creation (with matter — visible and dark — making up the remainder). Frieman embarked on what would become a two-decade mission to learn about dark energy by watching how it influences all that we can see: the Dark Energy Survey (DES).

Now that project has come to a close. In May 2026, DES shared findings based on its full dataset of thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies spanning billions of years of cosmic history. Those findings, in combination with data gathered by a different project, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), suggest that our understanding of what the universe is made of — the venerable “standard model” of cosmology — is not complete. “There appear to be cracks in that model,” said Simone Ferraro , a cosmologist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “There’s something that doesn’t fit.”

Joshua Frieman, a physicist now at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, co-founded the Dark Energy Survey to examine the accelerating expansion of the universe.

Cosmologists can’t yet say what that something is. What they can say is that after 20 years of stability, their field is returning to a state of confusion. “It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited,” Ferraro said.

Experimental cosmology is a piecemeal endeavor. It’s a bit like trying to reconstruct a person’s life from a dossier of data about them: report cards, utility bills, cholesterol tests, and so on. You come up with a story that weaves all the data together, go find new data, and use it to refine the story. Frieman and other cosmologists started to speculate about a missing form of energy in the mid-1990s because the story they were telling didn’t seem quite right.

In previous decades, they had peered at the sky and inferred roughly how much stuff was out there. They saw a smattering of galaxies lighting up the void — visible matter. Based on how fast the galaxies were spinning, astronomers deduced that a preponderance of invisible matter must surround each bright speck, holding it together — dark matter.

It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited.

The rate at which these galaxies were receding from view implied that the universe had been expanding for some 8 billion to 13 billion years. It looked as if there was just enough matter (dark and visible combined) to tug gravitationally on the universe and continuously slow this expansion without ever bringing it to a full halt.

But new observations started to clash with this accounting. Astronomers spotted stars, for instance, that seemed to be older than the universe. While trying to understand these and other anomalies, cosmologists noticed that it helped to add a new type of energy to their models.

items.title: The Intricate Textile Designs of William Morris Bring Into Conflict the Concepts of Art and Accessibility
items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: The 19th-century craftsman extolled the universal right to beauty. The problem was that his handmade items were necessarily expensive

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Arts & Culture
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Amy Crawford
Flora, designed by William Morris and Edward Coley Burne-Jones, made by William Knight, William Sleath and John Martin for Morris & Company,

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Born into a wealthy English family, William Morris (1834-1896) grew up in the countryside, honing a love for nature that found expression in fabric and wallpaper he designed for his successful firm, Morris & Company. An activist as well as an artist and businessman, he loathed the inequity of Victorian society and the soullessness of the industrial age, coming to embrace revolutionary socialism.

But while he believed in a universal right to beauty, his own careful craftsmanship held a certain contradiction, says Amy George, curator of a retrospective of Morris’ original designs opening this month at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England. “Anything handmade is expensive,” she notes. “And it should be expensive, because of the labor that goes into it.”

Perhaps ironically, in recent years capitalism has made Morris’ work more accessible, as it has appeared on products from mass-market brands like H&M and Williams Sonoma. In a way, it seems, his goal of art for all may finally have been realized.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

Amy Crawford is a Michigan-based freelance journalist writing about cities, science, the environment, art and education. A longtime Smithsonian contributor, her work also appears in CityLab and the Boston Globe .

items.title: The last klavern
items.author: Aeon Video
items.summary: Inside one of America’s last Ku Klux Klan halls, architects, historians and residents reckon with preserving Fort Worth’s past - by Aeon Video Watch on Aeon

images.caption: Photo of an abandoned brick building interior with graffiti and a reflection in a large puddle on the concrete floor.
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In Fort Worth, Texas, a massive, dilapidated building serves as an ever-present symbol of racial violence and segregation to those who know its history. Constructed in the 1920s, the structure, initially known as Klavern No 101 , was briefly the auditorium and headquarters of Fort Worth’s Ku Klux Klan chapter. It stood between downtown and the North Side, where migrants and communities of colour had settled, so many residents had to pass it on their way to work. In this short documentary, the director Chris Neighbors, a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, brings together scholars, community members and those directly involved in redesigning the space to reflect on its past and the thinking behind its transformation into an arts and community centre. Filmed inside the building itself, their conversations consider a question that extends far beyond Fort Worth: how do we preserve difficult histories without preserving the values they once stood for?

items.title: Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition?
items.author: Steven Strogatz and Janna Levin
items.summary: Albert-László Barabási explains how the same organizing principles shape everything from the internet to the cell, and how mapping the networks inside our bodies could change how we treat disease and think about food. The post Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

images.caption: Lámina de Quanta Magazine
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together. When researchers began mapping real-world networks in the 1990s – from the World Wide Web to Hollywood actors linked by films – they found that wildly different systems shared architectural features that their components alone could not explain. This suggested common organizing principles for how networks form and develop.

In this episode, two of the pioneers of network science – Albert-László Barabási and co-host Steven Strogatz – discuss how the field took shape, the ideas that underpin it, and why this is more than graph theory under a different name. The conversation then turns to health and nutrition. Disease-related genes cluster in “network neighborhoods”, Barabási explains, which may help identify better drug targets and predict which patients will respond to which drugs. That work led him to his Foodome project , which catalogs the molecules found in the food we eat and asks what they do inside our cells. By his count, around 135,000 compounds lie outside conventional nutrition, which concerns itself mainly with energy, building blocks, and vitamins. These compounds, which he calls the “dark matter of nutrition,” and their effects on the body are only beginning to be understood.

Listen on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , TuneIn or your favorite podcasting app, or you can stream it from Quanta .

LEVIN: A podcast… where… you can’t make me laugh, okay. A podcast from Quanta Magazine where we explore some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.

STROGATZ: Well, hey, Janna, I’m gonna take you back in a time warp to the 1990s. Do you wanna go there with me?

STROGATZ: There was a trend back then, where people would play a game that they called Six Degrees of Separation.

STROGATZ: Right. So if people don’t remember, Kevin Bacon, he was in a lot of movies and a game developed around him where you would name an actor, whoever, Marlon Brando or James Dean, and then you have to figure out a path of co-stars. You know, Marlon Brando was in such and such movie with somebody who was in a movie with Kevin Bacon. In that case, we would say Marlon Brando was two steps away. He had a Bacon number of two.

LEVIN: [ Laughs ] Right. Now, this though has some actual mathematical underpinnings. And as I remember, you did substantial work on some of this, how we’re all connected and how the world is smaller than we think, how that happens. You know, how do you… Do you know the guy Joe from Chicago? And you’re like, “Of course I know Joe.” Right?

STROGATZ: Well, it is true. My student Duncan Watts and I got very interested in the math of Six Degrees of Separation, like what would a network have to be like to have that property? And around that time, when we published our paper, soon after we heard from Malcolm Gladwell before he was really famous as Malcolm Gladwell, and he wanted to talk about this idea, and he ended up writing an article that was called Six Degrees of Lois Weisberg.

STROGATZ: Yeah, that’s the point. Everybody knows Lois. Lois knew everyone in Chicago and all over the place.

And so, we all know that there are these connectors in our networks, and that’s actually what we’re gonna be hearing about to some extent in this upcoming interview with László Barabási.

So, he is a network scientist at Northeastern University. He’s also got an appointment with Harvard Medical School and with the Central European University in Budapest, Hungary. And he has been looking at the role of what he calls hubs. You know, these outsized Lois Weisberg-like nodes in a network that seem to have a tremendous number of connections and the effect that they have on the behavior of the network as a result.

LEVIN: This probably has application for other complex systems than just human social systems?

items.title: Soldiers of Misfortune: The Drawings of Urs Graf the Elder
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: A mercenary and miscreant, the Swiss Renaissance artist Urs Graf lived the violence and vice he summoned on his drafting table. Miya Tokumitsu introduces us to his astonishing drawings of soldiers and sex workers, and finds an impotent melancholy within these often nightmarish scenes.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A mercenary and miscreant, the Swiss Renaissance artist Urs Graf lived the violence and vice he summoned on his drafting table. Miya Tokumitsu introduces us to his astonishing drawings of soldiers and sex workers, and finds an impotent melancholy within these often nightmarish scenes.

Urs Graf the Elder, Prostitute Inviting Love , 1514 — Source .

Many artists draw ably; a rarefied few draw with an animating touch that can imbue a single line with meaning, mood, and character. Some soft scribbles and scratches become an owl with a scowl full of menace and cynicism. A thatch of quick slashes forms a clump of grass that radiates the carnal energy of the figure before it, a young woman offering herself for sex. 1 These marks appear in the work of Urs Graf the Elder (ca. 1485–ca. 1528), one of the great maestros of the pen, who possessed one of the wilder imaginations of the sixteenth century. A mysterious and troubling figure, Graf bequeathed to the world a set of astonishing drawings filled with erotic-melancholic imagery : virile soldiers and wily prostitutes, with a supporting cast of satyrs, lecherous monks, and fools. His iconography reflects the context of Swiss martial culture during the Italian Wars of the early sixteenth century, interpreted via his self-consciously bizarre sensibility. Yet his compositions continue to fascinate due to their punchy, graphic style and their audacious visual meditations on sex and death. Centuries before Freud, Graf plumbed the far reaches of these fundamental human drives.

Born in Solothurn, Switzerland, around 1485, Graf was taught by his goldsmith father, Hug, from whom he presumably learned the fundamentals of design and draftsmanship in addition to metalwork techniques. As a young man, between 1503 and 1509, he worked as a designer of book illustrations in Strasbourg and as a goldsmith in Zürich, finally settling in Basel and establishing his own enterprise. In 1511, he married Sibylla von Brunn; their son was born the following year. While establishing his artistic career and family, Graf fought in at least four military campaigns as a Swiss mercenary, or Reisläufer : he set out to Rome with a troop from his hometown of Solothurn in 1511; joined a Basel expedition to Dijon in 1513; fought French and German forces at Marignano in 1515; and in 1521 marched on Milan and Bicocca. 2

Urs Graf the Elder, Standard-Bearer with His Page , 1516 — Source .

Urs Graf the Elder, Pyramus and Thisbe , 1525 — Source .

At home, Graf was a notorious and incorrigible miscreant. He was censured and jailed numerous times for transgressions that included: spousal battery; adultery and patronizing prostitutes; mocking and slandering local citizens including a priest, tailor, and coachmaker; and assaulting locals, often without apparent provocation. In 1518, he fled the city following an assault so violent that his victim was permanently disabled. He was permitted to return the following year, however, as the city was in need of a die-cutter for its mint and Graf’s talents proved too compelling for them to cancel him permanently. 3 Basel’s publishers, too, continued to seek his services as an illustrator. From 1527, documentation of Graf’s activity evaporates. Sibylla remarried in October 1528 (one hopes, to a nicer man), suggesting that Graf had died or disappeared from Basel by then. 4 That year, Graf would have been about forty-three years old.

Somehow, amid all his decamping for battle and local troublemaking, Graf managed to be a prolific and successful artist. If he were active today, he would surely qualify as a “multihyphenate creator”, skilled as he was in book illustration and single-sheet woodcut design, metalwork, stained glass production, engraving, and drawing. Graf also experimented in the novel technique of etching, which emerged around the 1510s. From his goldsmith training, he developed a keen sense of design and ornamental composition that disposed him favorably to the book publishers of Basel and Strasbourg who employed him as an illustrator. (That he evidently worked quickly was surely a boon, too.) Drawing was the medium in which Graf was truly groundbreaking, however. 5 He employed an eye-catching graphic style to depict vernacular subjects in transgressive scenarios; it is a visual strategy that remains effective still today, evident in the work of Kara Walker, who also reformulates figures and tropes from popular media like silhouettes and minstrel shows into nightmarish scenes.

Urs Graf the Elder, Woman with Child and Fool , 1525 — Source .

In one of Graf’s many drawings of sex work , a mercenary soldier and prostitute stand together as a couple, in a half embrace. This is no love match; wearing a weary expression, the woman fondles the man’s purse, which dangles from his neck just above his codpiece and a perpendicularly hanging sword. Gazing down at the coin bundle being evaluated, the man extends an open hand in a gesture of negotiation. Each person has something the other wants as well as their own risks to weigh. If rejected, the man suffers sexual humiliation. By issuing such a rejection, the woman risks provoking revenge in the form of battery and rape — a possibility suggested by the man’s burly physique and ample, priapic weaponry. She could become pregnant out of wedlock, a condition with its own jeopardies and burdens. The specter of venereal disease looms over both figures. The least harmful outcome seems a mutually agreeable exchange of sex for money in which both protagonists depart, health intact. But given that women in the sex trade at this time usually entered it for lack of other means of survival, such transactions were hardly made on equal terms. 6 Nevertheless, this woman has apparently made the best of her lot in life, as evidenced by her keys, heavy purse, and dagger — all common visual signifiers of a head of household during the early modern period. She is not entirely without power or authority.

Urs Graf the Elder, Soldier and Young Woman in a Landscape , ca. 1500–28 — Source .

Graf’s imagery opens a view onto the heady and hazard-filled world of the Swiss mercenary, a figure emblematic of political and social upheaval at the dawn of the modern era. It was the mercenary’s daily labor that implemented epochal shifts in war- and statecraft that emerged during the Renaissance. The Italian Wars (a yearslong mêlée that entangled Swiss, French, Italian, and German forces) engendered new methods of warfare that entailed larger-than-ever armies of professional troops, mostly infantry, skilled in modern weapons and tactics. 7 A two-sheet panoramic woodcut by Graf’s German contemporary, Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528), pictures a sixteenth-century fortress siege, complete with large, disciplined troop formations, heavy artillery, and the logistical coordination of massive baggage trains. This is not the kind of operation that can be carried out by a labor force significantly padded with pressed peasant boys and village layabouts. It required large numbers of competent, battle-hardened soldiers. This new way of making war, defined by the simultaneous professionalization and expansion of armies, came at an unprecedented financial cost, producing another now-familiar piece of state machinery: sprawling, sophisticated taxation and credit systems. 8

Albrecht Dürer, The Siege of a Fortress , date unknown — Source .

This modern warcraft shook up the Swiss social order. In 1477, Swiss pikemen surged into continental renown following their victory over Charles the Bold and his Burgundian knights in the Battle of Nancy. 9 Armies from all over Western Europe were keen to fill their ranks with Swiss recruits. Rather suddenly, a Swiss youth from the countryside, who had previously faced a future of cowherding, now had the opportunity to enjoy travel, adventure, sexual hijinks, and potential riches in the form of war booty. All he had to do was enlist with the recruiter passing through town. In fact, enough Swiss cowherds enlisted that their German battlefield antagonists, called Landsknechte (“servants of the land”), coined a panoply of cow-themed epithets to describe them: Kuhmäuler (cow mouths), Kuhbuben (cow boys), Kuhschwäntze (cow tails). 10 Mercenary culture quickly embedded itself into Swiss society, and it became common for men, urban and rural, to dabble in warfare for a campaign or two. 11 It was not only the uneducated or destitute who answered the calls to fight. Graf’s artist compatriot, Niklaus Manuel (ca. 1484–1530), also did some turns as a mercenary. In addition to his pursuits in the visual arts, Manuel was a playwright and member of the Bern civic council from 1510 until his death — a true Renaissance man. 12

items.title: The Triumph of Labour: Walter Crane’s Cartoons for the Cause (1896)
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: Socialist illustrations intended as party favours for participants in the International Workers’ Congress.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
By all accounts, the 1896 gathering of the International Workers’ Congress, held in London’s Queen’s Hall on Langham Place, was a chaotic affair . A surfeit of celebrities — George Bernard Shaw, Emmeline Pankhurst, Peter Kropotkin , Rosa Luxemburg, Clara Zetkin, Jean Jaurès — seems not to have quieted the tenor of the discussion. “It was Babel and Bedlam rolled into one”, the published proceedings admitted. At issue was the participation of anarchists in the activities of the Second International; ostensibly expelled at the 1893 Zurich Congress, several — including Kropotkin and Paul Delessalle — had snuck back in as trade unionists. Fights ensued, and from that point on, anarchism and socialism were more or less at odds.

At least, as the 775 delegates returned home, they could nurse their broken spirits with Cartoons for the Cause . The volume was compiled from images by the preeminent socialist illustrator Walter Crane, who wrote in a preface how he hoped the twelve plates, plus two poems and a “fable”, would

The collection brought together a selection of the political cartoons Crane had been publishing in the radical press — The Clarion , Justice , Commonweal — since 1885, plus an opening plate designed specially for the occasion: a handsome Englishman in a Phrygian cap, opening his arms to representatives of the twenty countries who were descending on the city. “International solidarity of labour”, the caption reads: “the true answer to ‘jingoism’”.

Other cartoons warned of dangers. “The Vampire”, one of Crane’s most famous images, shows a laborer collapsed on a pile of rubble, being savaged by a winged creature helpfully labeled “Religious Hypocrisy”, “Capitalism”, and “Party Politics”. Luckily, an avenging angel with the trumpet of Socialism is on her way. The following image shows an old woman (“Parliamentary Government”) hoarding land, capital, wages, profits, and tram shares from a begging child (“Unemployed”).

Nevertheless, it is in the inspirational images that one feels Crane’s fervency. A children’s book illustrator by trade, a doyen of the Arts and Crafts movement, and a latter-day Pre-Raphaelite , his style is better suited to the utopian images of the second half of the album. The socialist utopia of the Victorians was, Eric Hobsbawm wrote , replete with “imagery of spring and flowers, of harvest . . . of girls in light flowing dresses and Phrygian bonnets. Ceres was the goddess of communism.” The densely illustrated “Triumph of Labour” that Crane had designed for an 1891 May Day is a case in point: men on laden carts, chubby children with floral wreaths, the winged goddess of Victory at the lead. Despite the failure of the Paris Commune in 1871, Crane’s is a fundamentally optimistic vision, looking forward to a future of abundance for all.

(If you’d like to spread the cause a little further, we have a couple of Crane’s cartoons available as prints and Fair Wear t-shirts ( here and here ) in our shop. All proceeds go toward sustaining The Public Domain Review ’s own utopic project.)

items.title: D. W. Griffith’s A Corner in Wheat (1909)
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: D. W. Griffith’s moral tale of agricultural greed, borrowing from Frank Norris’ antimonopolist fictions.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

videos.caption: Reproductor audiovisual de la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A Corner in Wheat , directed by D. W. Griffith (American Mutoscope and Biograph Company, 1909).

We open on cropland. A farmer is running his hands through a bag of seed as his wife and daughter look on. Sowing season has come: it is time to plant this year’s wheat. He and an old man (his father?) walk slowly through a field, followed by a horse-driven plough. A cut: in a cushy office, a businessman — the “Wheat King”, surrounded by his lackeys — ponders the best way to get rich. The next scene, in the stock market, is announced by a card: “IN THE WHEAT PIT / THE FINAL THRESHING HAS ARRIVED.” What is getting beaten, however, is not the wheat itself but the king’s opponents. He has cornered the market, allowing him to set the commodity’s price: we next see a bakery, where the cost of bread has jumped from 5 cents to 10, and children are going hungry.

The simultaneous action of this 1909 short film helped forge the reputation of a young D. W. Griffith. Reportedly inspired in part by Charles Dickens’ narrative techniques, the director had developed a technique of parallel editing , allowing him to juxtapose different narratives to moral as well as dramatic ends. Intercut with the Wheat King’s feasting is the crushing poverty of the farm and the breadline. A somewhat heavy-handed message — some hamminess among the misérables doesn’t help — but one that probably bore repeating as the Gilded Age came to a close.

The film, produced for the Biograph Company, was based on the writings of the Progressive journalist and novelist Frank Norris, particularly his short story “ A Deal in Wheat ” (1903). But the narrative was given additional piquancy by an eerily similar scheme put in place by the Chicago businessman James A. Patten a few months earlier, which — as in the film — saw bread prices double.

In A Corner in Wheat , the Wheat King takes his family for a tour of the grain elevators where their ill-gotten wealth is stored. As they set off, he gets held behind, as his assistant hands him a letter from his accountant. We get to read it too: “Dear Sir:– You have control of the entire market of the world. Yesterday added $4,000,000 to your fortune.” Griffith actually underestimated what Patten’s profits would be: when the scheme finally collapsed in May 1909, the financier had made around $5,000,000 from his efforts — about $185,000,000 in today’s money.

However, while Patten emerged unscathed from his dealings, the Wheat King meets his punishment, this one taken from an earlier novel by Norris, The Octopus (1901). Jumping in joy at his new wealth, the Wheat King accidentally stumbles into a pit of threshed wheat, getting buried alive in the commodity that enriched him. He gets his comeuppance; but those who could not buy bread are still hungry, some killed by police during a riot. The last shot of the film reproduces the second: the farmer is walking in his field, sowing. But this time he is on his own. Maybe his father is dead; he certainly can no longer afford to hire a plough.

Norris died at thirty-two, leaving his planned Epic of the Wheat trilogy still unfinished. (His later reputation was tarnished by his virulent anti-Semitism; Griffith’s would, of course, be defined by the racism of The Birth of a Nation .) A Progressive, Norris hoped his writing would help awaken the working classes to their oppression. At the end of “A Deal in Wheat”, his financiers are perfectly well-off, but his farmer is not resigned:

Griffith was perhaps no less didactic. Parallel editing allowed his viewer, like the farmer, to see finance from the inside and the outside, from top and bottom — a new perspective gained at the cost of a 7 cent movie ticket.

items.title: The Race to the Origin: The Letters That Helped Secure Darwin’s Place in the History of Evolution
items.author: Diane M. Rielinger
items.summary: How do we know who was first to make a scientific discovery? Explore how Charles Darwin's correspondence with Harvard botanist Asa Gray helped establish his priority in developing the theory of evolution by natural selection, and how historical letters preserved in BHL illuminate pivotal moments in the history of scien

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

Science is often characterized as moving in slow motion, with experiments yielding small incremental steps. However, as information is shared and knowledge coalesces, multiple scientists can converge on a “eureka” moment nearly simultaneously. So who gets the credit for the big discoveries and who becomes the footnote? How do you prove who was first?

Charles Darwin (1809–1882), like many of his contemporaries, was a voracious correspondent with other scientists. These scientists shared thoughts and ideas via letters over many years as theories were debated and refined. Darwin’s correspondence with Harvard botanist Asa Gray (1810–1888), particularly a September 5, 1857 letter and enclosure from Darwin that is held at the Harvard University Botany Libraries and available in BHL, would prove vital in demonstrating Darwin’s priority for the theory of evolution over fellow Englishman Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913).

Left: Asa Gray, c. 1865–1867. Unique ID 0946. Right: Charles Darwin, 1861. Unique IDs DC04, 0074, 0089. Both images from the Botany Libraries photograph collection, circa 1770–2020. gra00083. Botany Libraries, Harvard University.

In the mid-1850s, scientists were struggling with questions related to the origin and distribution of species and their variations. The great explorations around the world, coupled with modern classification systems, provided a wealth of data to evaluate and debate prevailing theories. Particularly difficult to explain were geographically isolated species and widespread but geographically disjointed species. So what was the “origin of species”?

In 1854, Charles Darwin was contemplating several components of the “origin” question. Darwin’s extensive work on barnacles, summarized in A monograph on the sub-class Cirripedia, with figures of all the species , demonstrated that a large amount of variation existed that was not well explained by a popular theory that life emerged from a single location on Earth.

Intrigued by Gray’s insights into Flora Novae-Zelandiae that Joseph Dalton Hooker (1817–1911) shared with him, Darwin contacted Gray directly on April 25, 1855 with questions about alpine flora species and distributions outlined in Gray’s Manual of the Botany of the Northern United States (see also Darwin’s annotated copy of the 1856 2nd edition). Thus began a years-long correspondence that expanded from data requests to philosophical discussions and influenced Darwin’s theory of evolution.

After three years of correspondence, Darwin shared with Gray in a July 20, 1857, letter :

“Nineteen years (!) ago it occurred to me that whilst attention employed on Natural History I might perhaps do good if I noted any sort of facts bearing on the question on the origin of species; and this I have since been doing. Either species have been independently created, or they have descended from other species, like varieties from one species… I must tell you that I have come to the relentless conclusion that there are no such things as independently created species, the species are only strongly defined varieties.”

Gray responded in August 1857 (complete letter not available), and Darwin followed up with the September 5, 1857 , letter that included an enclosure with his six-points establishing the theory of evolution by natural selection.

Charles Darwin letter to Asa Gray, September 5, 1857 . Asa Gray correspondence files of the Gray Herbarium, 1820–1931. gra00078. Botany Libraries, Harvard University.

With his theory still unpublished but documented in correspondence, Darwin received a package on June 18, 1858, from Alfred Russel Wallace expressing similar theories. In a letter dated July 4, 1858 , Darwin asked Gray to confirm his receipt of the September 5, 1857 letter and enclosure to establish his priority for the theory of evolution by natural selection .

The “ Darwin-Wallace paper ” was published in 1858 by the Linnean Society with the assistance of Joseph Dalton Hooker and Charles Lyell. The paper contains three items:

“In June 1842 I first allowed myself the satisfaction of writing a very brief abstract of my theory in pencil in 34 pages and this was enlarged during the summer of 1844 into one of 230 pages, which I had fairly copied out and still possess.”
